Willis Tower. Formerly the Sears Tower, this 110-story skyscraper was completed in 1973 in Chicago, rising 1,450 feet and holding the record as the world's tallest building for twenty-five years. Its bundled-tube structural system and striking black facade made it an architectural and engineering milestone of the nineteen-seventies. Designed by the firm Skidmore, Owings and Merrill and completed in just over three years despite Chicago's harsh winter conditions during construction, the tower employs a novel bundled-tube structural system of nine square tubes clustered together. This allows the tower to sway in wind while maintaining stability, a paradigm shift in tall-building engineering. It is clad in black anodized aluminum and black granite, giving it a distinctive visual presence distinct from the lighter-colored towers of Manhattan. At 1,450 feet to the roof, it surpassed the Empire State Building at 1,250 feet and held the world record until the Burj Khalifa was completed in 2010. Originally built as the global headquarters of Sears, Roebuck and Company, the company's decline left much of the office space vacant by the 2000s. The Skydeck observation deck on the one-hundred-third floor remains a major Chicago tourist attraction, offering 360-degree views across Lake Michigan and the city.
